ukmt-jmc-2026-01.title: Work them out
ukmt-jmc-2026-01.body:
Remember to multiply before adding: A $= 0+26 = 26$, B $= 2+0+12 = 14$, C $= 46$, D $= 40-6 = 34$, E $= 20+12 = 32$. The largest is C.

**Answer: (C) $20+26$**

ukmt-jmc-2026-01.title: Compare with C
ukmt-jmc-2026-01.body:
C is $20+26$. E is $20+12$, smaller. A is just $26$. D is $40-6 = 34 < 46$. B is tiny. So C is largest.

**Answer: (C) $20+26$**

ukmt-jmc-2026-02.title: Count the edges
ukmt-jmc-2026-02.body:
Four separate squares would have $4\times4 = 16$ cm of edges. Every place where two squares share a side removes $2$ cm. In A, B, C and E the squares touch along $3$ sides, giving $16-6 = 10$ cm. In D (a $2\times2$ square) they touch along $4$ sides, giving $16-8 = 8$ cm.

**Answer: (D)**

ukmt-jmc-2026-02.title: Trace the outline
ukmt-jmc-2026-02.body:
Figure D is a $2$ cm by $2$ cm square with perimeter $8$ cm. Walking round each of the others gives $10$ cm (e.g. C is a $4\times1$ strip: $4+1+4+1 = 10$).

**Answer: (D)**

ukmt-jmc-2026-03.title: Calculate
ukmt-jmc-2026-03.body:
Top: $4-3-2-1 = -2$. Bottom: $8-7-6-5 = -10$. So the value is $\frac{-2}{-10} = \frac15$.

**Answer: (B) $\frac15$**

ukmt-jmc-2026-03.title: Rewrite the subtractions
ukmt-jmc-2026-03.body:
Top $= 4-(3+2+1) = 4-6$, bottom $= 8-(7+6+5) = 8-18$. That's $\frac{-2}{-10} = \frac15$ (negative divided by negative is positive).

**Answer: (B) $\frac15$**

ukmt-jmc-2026-04.title: Add the fractions
ukmt-jmc-2026-04.body:
$\frac12+\frac13+\frac14 = \frac{6+4+3}{12} = \frac{13}{12}$. So $\frac{13}{12}$ of the number is $52$; $\frac1{12}$ of it is $4$, and the number is $48$.

**Answer: (E) 48**

ukmt-jmc-2026-05.title: Estimate
ukmt-jmc-2026-05.body:
From 1956 to 2026 is $70$ years. The clock strikes $24$ times a day, about $365$ days a year:
$$24\times365\times70 \approx 24\times350\times70 = 24\times24\,500 \approx 600\,000.$$

**Answer: (D) 600 000**

ukmt-jmc-2026-05.title: Hours per year
ukmt-jmc-2026-05.body:
A year has about $365\times24 \approx 8760$ hours, roughly $9000$. Over $70$ years: about $9000\times70 = 630\,000$, closest to $600\,000$.

**Answer: (D) 600 000**

ukmt-jmc-2026-06.title: List them
ukmt-jmc-2026-06.body:
Three-digit numbers with digits $0$ or $1$ (first digit can't be $0$): $100, 101, 110, 111$, sum $422$. Two-digit numbers with digits $2$ or $3$: $22, 23, 32, 33$, sum $110$. Total $422+110 = 532$.

**Answer: (C) 532**

ukmt-jmc-2026-06.title: Add by place value
ukmt-jmc-2026-06.body:
Monday: all four numbers have hundreds digit $1$ ($400$); tens digit $1$ in two of them ($20$); units digit $1$ in two ($2$): $422$. Tuesday: tens digits $2,2,3,3$ total $10$ tens $= 100$; units the same, total $10$: $110$. So $532$.

**Answer: (C) 532**

ukmt-jmc-2026-07.title: Odd and even
ukmt-jmc-2026-07.body:
Every prime except $2$ is odd, and five odd numbers add up to an odd number. $2026$ is even, so one of the primes must be $2$ – and $2$ is the smallest prime. So the smallest prime is always $2$: one possibility. (Such lists exist, e.g. $2+19+31+983+991 = 2026$.)

**Answer: (A) one**

ukmt-jmc-2026-07.title: What if 2 is missing?
ukmt-jmc-2026-07.body:
If $2$ were not in the list, all five primes would be odd and the total would be odd, not $2026$. If $2$ is in the list, it must be the smallest. Either way the smallest prime is $2$. So there is exactly one possibility.

**Answer: (A) one**

ukmt-jmc-2026-08.title: Shorten each side by 3
ukmt-jmc-2026-08.body:
The square has side $3$ cm. Rectangle $TVRW$ has each side $3$ cm shorter than the matching side of $PQRS$ (we cut off a $3$ cm strip from the top and from the left). Its perimeter is $30-4\times3 = 18$ cm.

**Answer: (C) 18 cm**

ukmt-jmc-2026-08.title: Use length + width
ukmt-jmc-2026-08.body:
For $PQRS$, length $+$ width $= 15$ cm. For $TVRW$ it is $(\text{length}-3)+(\text{width}-3) = 9$ cm, so its perimeter is $18$ cm.

**Answer: (C) 18 cm**

ukmt-jmc-2026-09.title: Blocks of 15
ukmt-jmc-2026-09.body:
In each block of $15$ numbers, $5$ are multiples of $3$, $3$ are multiples of $5$, and $1$ ($15$) is both, so $15-5-3+1 = 8$ are said. The first block $1$–$15$ gives $8$ numbers; the next $7$ come from $16$–$30$: $16, 17, 19, 22, 23, 26, 28$. The 15th is $28$.

**Answer: (D) 28**

ukmt-jmc-2026-10.title: Corresponding angles
ukmt-jmc-2026-10.body:
$IH \parallel JK$ and $GHK$ is a straight line, so $\angle GHI = \angle JKH = 80^\circ$ (corresponding angles). In the kite, the angles at $G$ and $I$ between unequal sides are equal: $\angle FIH = \angle FGH = 85^\circ$. The angles of quadrilateral $FGHI$ add to $360^\circ$:
$$\angle IFG = 360-80-85-85 = 110^\circ.$$

**Answer: (B) $110^\circ$**

ukmt-jmc-2026-10.title: Via the parallelogram
ukmt-jmc-2026-10.body:
In parallelogram $HIJK$, neighbouring angles add to $180^\circ$, so $\angle IHK = 180-80 = 100^\circ$. On the straight line $GHK$, $\angle GHI = 180-100 = 80^\circ$. Then as before $\angle IFG = 360-80-2\times85 = 110^\circ$.

**Answer: (B) $110^\circ$**

ukmt-jmc-2026-11.title: Total of all the digits
ukmt-jmc-2026-11.body:
The nine digits add up to $45$, which is odd. If every row had an even sum, the three row sums would add to an even number – but they add to $45$. Impossible, so there are $0$ ways.

**Answer: (A) 0**

ukmt-jmc-2026-11.title: Compare rows and columns
ukmt-jmc-2026-11.body:
The three row sums and the three column sums both add up to the grand total. Three even row sums give an even total, while three odd column sums give an odd total. The same number can't be both, so no arrangement works.

**Answer: (A) 0**

ukmt-jmc-2026-12.title: Eat along the lines of symmetry
ukmt-jmc-2026-12.body:
The array has four lines of symmetry: the middle row, the middle column and the two diagonals. These lines contain $5+5+5+5-3 = 17$ biscuits (the centre is on all four).

Eating biscuits on one line of symmetry keeps that line a line of symmetry. Once a whole line is eaten, the remaining array is still symmetric about the perpendicular line (which goes through the gap), so he can then eat along that, and so on through all four lines: $17$ biscuits.

The other $8$ biscuits (two in each corner region, like a knight's move from the centre) come in pairs matched by every one of these symmetries, and no other line of symmetry is possible for the remaining set, so removing any one of them would leave no line of symmetry. So $17$ is the maximum.

**Answer: (D) 17**

ukmt-jmc-2026-12.title: Why not more than 17?
ukmt-jmc-2026-12.body:
Number the rows and columns $1$ to $5$. After the $17$ biscuits on the four symmetry lines are eaten, the $8$ left are at $(1,2), (2,1), (1,4), (2,5), (4,1), (5,2), (4,5), (5,4)$. A pattern in a $5\times5$ grid can only be symmetric about the middle row, the middle column or a diagonal. Removing, say, $(1,2)$ breaks all four: its mirror images $(5,2)$, $(1,4)$, $(2,1)$ and $(4,5)$ are still there. The same happens for any of the eight, so John must stop at $25-8 = 17$.

**Answer: (D) 17**

ukmt-jmc-2026-13.title: Find p first
ukmt-jmc-2026-13.body:
'$pq$' $+$ '$pr$' $= 20p+q+r$. Since $q+r \le 18$: if $p = 2$ the sum is at most $58$; if $p = 4$ it is at least $80$. So $p = 3$, and $q+r = 75-60 = 15$. Then $p+q+r = 18$.

**Answer: (E) 18**

ukmt-jmc-2026-13.title: An example
ukmt-jmc-2026-13.body:
Try $37+38 = 75$: $p = 3$, $q = 7$, $r = 8$, giving $18$. (Other possibilities like $36+39$ also give $18$, since $20p+q+r = 75$ forces $p = 3$, $q+r = 15$.)

**Answer: (E) 18**

ukmt-jmc-2026-14.title: Add the two small perimeters
ukmt-jmc-2026-14.body:
The perimeters of $RPS$ and $RSQ$ together use $RP$, $PS$, $SQ$, $QR$ – the whole perimeter of $PQR$ – plus $RS$ twice. So $44+60 = 80+2\,RS$, giving $RS = 12$ cm.

**Answer: (E) 12 cm**

ukmt-jmc-2026-14.title: Name the sides
ukmt-jmc-2026-14.body:
Let $RP = a$, $PS = b$, $SQ = c$, $QR = d$, $RS = x$. Then $a+b+c+d = 80$, $a+b+x = 44$, $c+d+x = 60$. Adding the last two: $80+2x = 104$, so $x = 12$.

**Answer: (E) 12 cm**

ukmt-jmc-2026-15.title: Fold it
ukmt-jmc-2026-15.body:
Put face 2 at the front. Then 3 folds to the bottom, 5 to the back, the left-arrow face to the left side, the right-arrow face (attached to 3) to the right side, and 1 (attached to the top of the left face) to the top.

The left arrow points away from face 2, across the left face, to its far edge, which meets the back face $5$. The right arrow points away from face 3, up the right face, to its far edge, which meets the top face $1$. The sum is $5+1 = 6$.

**Answer: (D) 6**

ukmt-jmc-2026-15.title: Opposite faces
ukmt-jmc-2026-15.body:
In the net, $2$ and $5$ are opposite (two apart in a column), and so are $1$ and $3$. Each arrow points away from the numbered face its square is attached to, so after folding it points to the face opposite that one. The left-arrow square is attached to $2$, so its arrow points to $5$; the right-arrow square is attached to $3$, so its arrow points to $1$. Sum $6$.

**Answer: (D) 6**

ukmt-jmc-2026-16.title: Odd and even
ukmt-jmc-2026-16.body:
All the sums are at least $3$, so they must be odd primes; hence neighbours have opposite parity: odd and even numbers alternate around the ring. Since $1$ is odd and $x$ is opposite it (three steps away), $x$ is even, and the two circles next to $x$ hold the odd numbers $3$ and $5$.

$x$ can't be $4$ ($4+5 = 9$) or $6$ ($6+3 = 9$). So $x = 2$ ($2+3 = 5$, $2+5 = 7$, both prime). A full solution: going round, $1, 4, 3, 2, 5, 6$.

**Answer: (A) 2**

ukmt-jmc-2026-16.title: Check each option
ukmt-jmc-2026-16.body:
Odd/even must alternate, so $x$ is even: $2, 4$ or $6$. Its two neighbours are $3$ and $5$. Only $2$ makes primes with both ($5$ and $7$); $4+5$ and $6+3$ are $9$. A check of all arrangements confirms $x = 2$ every time.

**Answer: (A) 2**

ukmt-jmc-2026-17.title: Split by the start
ukmt-jmc-2026-17.body:
He must start with $1$.
- Start $10$: the next digit must be $1$ ($100$ breaks the rule). Then $101$ can be completed as $101100$ or $101010$: $2$ ways.
- Start $11$: the third $1$ can go in position 3, 4 or 5: $111000$, $110100$, $110010$: $3$ ways.

Total $5$.

**Answer: (B) 5**

ukmt-jmc-2026-17.title: Keep a running count
ukmt-jmc-2026-17.body:
Read the digits left to right, keeping a running count (1s minus 0s) never below $0$: $111000, 110100, 110010, 101100, 101010$. Any other order makes the count drop below $0$ at some point. So $5$.

**Answer: (B) 5**

ukmt-jmc-2026-18.title: Not all five, but four works
ukmt-jmc-2026-18.body:
If Amy and Bob both tell the truth, then Amy > Bob > Dan, so Dan can't have more than Amy and Dan's statement is false. So not all five can be true.

Four can be true: let Eve, Amy, Bob, Cat, Dan have $5, 4, 3, 2, 1$ pencils. Then Amy > Bob ✓, Bob > Cat and Dan ✓, Cat > Dan ✓, Eve > Amy ✓ (only Dan's statement is false).

**Answer: (D) 4**

ukmt-jmc-2026-18.title: Look for a contradiction cycle
ukmt-jmc-2026-18.body:
Amy says A > B, Bob says B > D (part of his statement), Dan says D > A. These three can't all hold (A > B > D > A is impossible), so at least one statement is false: at most $4$. The example $E > A > B > C > D$ shows $4$ is possible.

**Answer: (D) 4**

ukmt-jmc-2026-19.title: Name the three parts
ukmt-jmc-2026-19.body:
Let $\angle QPT = x$, $\angle TPS = y$, $\angle SPR = z$, with $x+y+z = 100$.

$QP = QS$, so triangle $QPS$ is isosceles and $\angle QSP = \angle QPS = x+y$. $RP = RT$, so $\angle RTP = \angle RPT = y+z$.

In triangle $PTS$: $y + (y+z) + (x+y) = 180$, i.e. $(x+y+z) + 2y = 180$, so $2y = 80$ and $y = 40^\circ$. It doesn't depend on the other angles.

**Answer: (C) $40^\circ$**

ukmt-jmc-2026-19.title: Use the angles of the big triangle
ukmt-jmc-2026-19.body:
Let $\angle Q = q$ and $\angle R = r$, with $q+r = 80$. In isosceles triangle $QPS$, $\angle QSP = \frac{180-q}{2}$; in isosceles triangle $RPT$, $\angle RTP = \frac{180-r}{2}$. In triangle $PTS$,
$$\angle TPS = 180 - \frac{180-q}{2} - \frac{180-r}{2} = \frac{q+r}{2} = 40^\circ.$$

**Answer: (C) $40^\circ$**

ukmt-jmc-2026-20.title: Combine the ratios
ukmt-jmc-2026-20.body:
Chocolate : cherry $= 7 : 6 = 35 : 30$. Cherry : cream $= 5 : 4 = 30 : 24$. Cream : coffee $= 3 : 2 = 24 : 16$. So chocolate : cherry : cream : coffee $= 35 : 30 : 24 : 16$, with total $105$ parts. These numbers have no common factor, so the total must be a multiple of $105$. Only $420 = 4\times105$ is (with $140, 120, 96, 64$ cakes).

**Answer: (E) 420**

ukmt-jmc-2026-20.title: Start from the coffee cakes
ukmt-jmc-2026-20.body:
If there are $n$ coffee cakes, there are $\frac{3n}{2}$ cream, $\frac54\cdot\frac{3n}{2} = \frac{15n}{8}$ cherry and $\frac76\cdot\frac{15n}{8} = \frac{35n}{16}$ chocolate cakes. The total is $\frac{105n}{16}$, and $n$ must be a multiple of $16$, so the total is a multiple of $105$: $420$ (with $n = 64$).

**Answer: (E) 420**

ukmt-jmc-2026-21.title: Use areas
ukmt-jmc-2026-21.body:
Let the big rectangle be $4x$ by $5x$ and use $k$ tiles: $20x^2 = 150k$, so $2x^2 = 15k$. Then $x^2$ is a multiple of $15$, so $x$ is a multiple of $15$ (as $3$ and $5$ are prime). The smallest is $x = 15$, giving $k = \frac{2\times225}{15} = 30$.

This works: the $60$ cm by $75$ cm rectangle can be made from two rows of $15$ tiles standing upright ($15\times5 = 75$ cm wide, $30$ cm tall each).

**Answer: (B) 30**

ukmt-jmc-2026-21.title: Think about the sides
ukmt-jmc-2026-21.body:
Each side of the big rectangle is made of tile edges ($5$ or $30$ cm), so both sides are multiples of $5$: $4x$ and $5x$ multiples of $5$ means $x$ is a multiple of $5$. Testing $x = 5$ ($20\times25$, area $500$) and $x = 10$ ($40\times50$, area $2000$): neither area is a multiple of the tile area $150$. $x = 15$ gives $60\times75 = 4500 = 30\times150$, and the arrangement above shows it can be done. So $30$ tiles.

**Answer: (B) 30**

ukmt-jmc-2026-22.title: Multiples of 5 and 7
ukmt-jmc-2026-22.body:
The number of frogs is a multiple of $5$ and the number of snakes a multiple of $7$. So the total is (multiple of $5$) $+$ (multiple of $7$):
- $22 = 15+7$
- $24 = 10+14$
- $26 = 5+21$
- $27 = 20+7$

For $23$: subtracting $0, 7, 14, 21$ leaves $23, 16, 9, 2$, none a multiple of $5$. So $23$ is impossible.

**Answer: (B) 23**

ukmt-jmc-2026-23.title: Compare the totals
ukmt-jmc-2026-23.body:
Call the numbers $p < q < r < s < t$. Then $p+q+r+s = 20$ and $q+r+s+t = 28$. Subtracting, $t-p = 8$, which is the range.

**Answer: (E) 8**

ukmt-jmc-2026-23.title: An example
ukmt-jmc-2026-23.body:
Try $2, 4, 6, 8, 10$: first four have mean $5$, last four have mean $7$, and the range is $10-2 = 8$. (The first solution shows the range is always $8$.)

**Answer: (E) 8**

ukmt-jmc-2026-24.title: Use the line total
ukmt-jmc-2026-24.body:
The two lines together contain all nine numbers, with $N$ counted twice: total $45+N$. Each line is half of this, so $N$ is odd and each line totals $\frac{45+N}{2}$.

The line through $6$ and $8$, $3$ has one empty square $m$: $6+m+N+8+3 = \frac{45+N}{2}$.
- $N = 1$: total $23$, $m = 5$ ✓
- $N = 3$: already used ✗
- $N = 5$: total $25$, $m = 3$ – already used ✗
- $N = 7$: total $26$, $m = 2$ ✓
- $N = 9$: total $27$, $m = 1$ ✓

In each good case the other four numbers fill the second line correctly (its total is automatically right). So $N$ can be $1, 7, 9$, with sum $17$.

**Answer: (A) 17**

ukmt-jmc-2026-24.title: Check by computer-style search
ukmt-jmc-2026-24.body:
Trying every way to put the six remaining numbers into the six empty squares and keeping those with equal line totals, the centre $N$ only ever takes the values $1$, $7$ and $9$. Their sum is $17$.

**Answer: (A) 17**

ukmt-jmc-2026-25.title: No tie or one tie
ukmt-jmc-2026-25.body:
(Here "at most two tied" means there is at most one tie, between two runners.)

**No ties:** $4\times3\times2\times1 = 24$ orders.

**One tie between two runners:** choose the pair in $6$ ways ($PQ, PR, PS, QR, QS, RS$). Treat the tied pair as one "block"; then there are $3$ things to put in order: $3\times2\times1 = 6$ ways. That's $6\times6 = 36$.

Total $24+36 = 60$.

**Answer: (B) 60**

ukmt-jmc-2026-25.title: Place the tied pair
ukmt-jmc-2026-25.body:
With a tie, there are three finishing positions. Choose which position the tied pair has ($3$ ways), which pair it is ($6$ ways), and the order of the other two runners in the remaining positions ($2$ ways): $3\times6\times2 = 36$. Adding the $24$ orders with no tie gives $60$.

**Answer: (B) 60**
